verses.note: Scripture says both that God regretted (here and 1 Samuel 15:11, 35) and that he is not a man that he should change his mind (1 Samuel 15:29, Numbers 23:19), sometimes in the same chapter. Classical theology reads such language as describing God's real opposition to evil in terms human beings can grasp, without implying that God was surprised or that his purpose failed; other theologians give the language more literal weight. All agree the verse forbids picturing God as indifferent.

God binds his future actions to a visible sign and speaks of remembering it. The language is deliberately human, but the point is his faithfulness: God places his own word where he will see it and pledges to act according to it.

The verse shows God's patience. He waits four centuries rather than act before judgment is just, which is the same forbearance the New Testament describes as meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4, 2 Peter 3:9).
God's knowledge is not presented here as abstract all-knowing but as attention: he sees a particular person in a particular place. Psalm 139 develops the same thought in prayer.
The question ties God's power to his promise. God is not described as able to do anything at all in the abstract, but as able to do what he has said, even when nature says otherwise.
Abraham's argument assumes that God's justice is not arbitrary but recognizable: humans made in his image can appeal to it. Deuteronomy 32:4 confesses the same conviction.
God's faithfulness is shown here as the exact match between what he says and what he does. The verse repeats the point twice so that no reader can miss that the birth is the keeping of a word.

Jacob names God's covenant love (chesed) and faithfulness (emet) as the explanation of his whole life. They are the qualities God will proclaim as his name at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), and Jacob confesses them here as things he has received, not earned.

The four verbs describe a God who is attentive, faithful to his word, and personally concerned with human suffering. Remembering, in Scripture, means turning to act on a commitment, not recalling forgotten information.

The God of Exodus is not unmoved by pain. He sees affliction, hears cries, and knows sufferings, and this knowledge leads to action. The verse is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of God's compassion joined to his power.

Christian theology has drawn the doctrine of God's self-existence (often called aseity) partly from this verse: God is not caused, completed, or sustained by anything outside himself. Jesus' words ‘before Abraham was born, I am’ (John 8:58) are widely read as an echo of this self-designation.

God's anger is real, and it is also slow and restrained: he does not reject Moses but provides for his weakness. Later God will describe himself as slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (34:6), and this scene is an early instance of it.

God's jealousy is the zeal of a covenant partner for an exclusive relationship. It is inseparable from his loving devotion: the same God who will not share his people with idols keeps faith with them for a thousand generations. The proportion of the two clauses is itself a statement about his character.

God describes himself, and mercy comes first and at length. Every term but the last is a form of love or grace, and the list became Israel's creed about God's character, quoted by psalmists and prophets across centuries.

Forgiveness and justice stand in the same sentence without canceling each other. The verse leaves the tension unresolved; the rest of Scripture, and for Christians the cross above all (Romans 3:25-26), shows how God can be both the one who forgives and the one who does not declare the guilty innocent.

The same God who has just proclaimed himself compassionate and gracious now calls himself Jealous. The two belong together: God's jealousy is the exclusive devotion of love, which refuses to share the beloved with rivals who would destroy her.
